formation.title: The Aragonese Empire
formation.text:
From Barcelona's quay the king's galley flies the Senyera Reial, four red bars on gold that the chroniclers say were drawn in royal blood. Naples bows. Palermo bows. Cagliari, Palma, Valencia, Zaragoza all wait on the verdict. The Crown of Aragon, four kingdoms and three duchies bound only by a peripatetic sovereign and the Consolat de Mar, has reached a moment its rivals dread: a single ruler, a single court, a single project that is no longer postponed.

The royal council asks what the project shall be. The Catalan merchants want a Mediterranean lake: Athens recovered, Egypt courted, the consulates reinforced from Bruges to Trebizond, the Almogavars on retainer, the four bars flying over every harbour where bills of exchange are settled. The Aragonese nobility and the new Trastamara administrators see otherwise: westward, toward an Iberia unified on the crown's terms before Castile can do it on theirs. Both paths are real. Alfonso the Magnanimous truly did pivot east; the Compromise of Caspe truly did seat us in the Iberian dynastic web. The court must choose which Aragon survives.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Mediterraneum Aragonense: let the sea be ours

modifiers.name: Mediterraneum Aragonense
modifiers.text: The crown looks east. Catalan consulates from Bruges to Constantinople, Almogavar mercenaries selling their billhooks to any prince who would pay them, and the four-bar Senyera Reial flying over a Mediterranean sea that has become an Aragonese lake. Naval primacy, mercenary depth, cosmopolitan culture and outward-looking diplomacy at the price of accepting the sea-divided polity rather than welding it inland.

modifiers.name: Hispano-Aragonese Crown
modifiers.text: If Iberia must be unified, let it be unified eastward. The crown turns its administrative weight inland: integrating Castilian and Andalusian populations, professionalizing the levies, and using the inheritance machinery of Trastamara dynastic politics to do to Castile what Castile did to us in another timeline. Manpower depth, cheap annexations, control consolidation, at the price of belligerent posture and centralizing reform.

advances.name: Pacta Conventa
advances.text: The Privilegio General of 1283 and the Aragonese coronation oath bind the crown to the constitutional pacts of the kingdom. The famous formula ('we, who are worth as much as you and together more than you, accept you as our king and lord, provided you observe our liberties and laws; if not, no') is unprecedented in Christian Europe.

advances.name: Llibre del Consolat de Mar
advances.text: The compiled Catalan maritime code is adopted from Marseille to Acre as the lex maritima of the Mediterranean. The Crown of Aragon owns no monopoly on the trade itself, yet every commercial dispute heard in any consulate is settled by Aragonese-Catalan rules.

event.title: The Llibre del Consolat de Mar
event.text: Centuries of Catalan maritime custom have been compiled into the Llibre del Consolat de Mar, the most comprehensive private law of shipping yet written in Christian Europe. Marseille adopts it. Pisa adopts it. Acre, Trapani, Famagusta, Bruges: wherever ships of the four bars dock, the Consolat is the law that decides who pays for jettison, who insures the cargo, who arbitrates between captain and merchant. The crown owns no monopoly on the trade itself, but every dispute brought before any consul anywhere is settled by Aragonese-Catalan rules.

advances.name: Catalan Company in Greece
advances.text: Roger de Flor's Almogavars take service with Byzantium in 1303, then carve out the Duchies of Athens and Neopatras for the Aragonese crown, the first Iberian power projection into the eastern Mediterranean and the model for two centuries of Catalan mercenary enterprise.

advances.name: Almudín de Valencia
advances.text: Valencia's great covered grain market, the Almudín, becomes the food spine of the Crown's Mediterranean campaigning. Centralized granary administration grants the kingdom an army-supply edge unmatched in 14th-century Iberia.

advances.name: Catalan Atlas
advances.text: The 1375 Catalan Atlas of the Cresques family makes Aragonese-Mallorcan cartography the most advanced of any Christian state. Pilots from Genoa and Venice quietly request copies; the kingdom's mariners hold a generation's lead in maritime intelligence.

event.title: The Cresques Atlas
event.text: The Jewish cartographer Cresques Abraham of Mallorca and his son Jafuda have completed the world atlas commissioned by Pere III. Six folio panels of vellum show the Mediterranean in unprecedented portolan detail, the African gold caravans of Mansa Musa, and the silk routes east as far as Cathay. The work is a wedding gift to the king of France: diplomacy and reconnaissance in one. No other Christian court has anything comparable. Pilots from Genoa and Venice quietly request copies. The Crown's mariners have a head start of a generation.

modifiers.name: Cresques Cartographic Project
modifiers.text: The Cresques family of Mallorca have set the world to parchment. Sea-kingdoms half a century ahead of their rivals in maritime presence and exploration.

advances.name: Compromise of Caspe
advances.text: The 1412 succession crisis is resolved when nine arbiters elect a new king in legal procedure rather than by sword. The settlement permanently changes how the Aragonese crown understands legitimacy: by pact, by election, by binding sentence.

event.title: The Compromise of Caspe
event.text:
Marti the Humane has died at Poblet without a legitimate heir. The crown stands vacant and five claimants press their cases: among them Ferdinand of Antequera, Castilian-born Trastamara prince and victor over Granada, and Jaume of Urgell, the native Catalan candidate descended in the male line from Jaume II. Nine arbiters from Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia have gathered at Caspe to render a binding judgement. The court awaits the king's preference, knowing the arbiters' sentence is secretly malleable.

Ferdinand brings dynastic weight, Castilian alliance, and the prestige of the recent Granadan campaigns. Jaume brings the loyalty of the Catalan nobility and the unbroken line of the Casa d'Arago. The choice will define whether the crown faces inward toward Iberian dynastic politics, or outward toward Catalan particularism.

options.text: Crown Ferdinand of Antequera: dynasty above all

modifiers.name: Trastamara Legitimacy
modifiers.text: Nine arbiters meeting at Caspe in 1412 chose Ferdinand of Antequera, the Castilian-born Trastamara prince, as legitimate heir to the Aragonese throne. The choice for dynastic continuity binds the crown into the Iberian succession network for centuries to come.

options.text: Crown Jaume of Urgell: the line stays Catalan

modifiers.name: House of Urgell Vindicated
modifiers.text: The Compromise of Caspe goes the other way: Jaume II of Urgell, the native Catalan claimant, takes the throne. The pactist nobles and the great cities of the Crown declare their privileges affirmed against any future foreign succession.

advances.name: Court of the Magnanimous
advances.text: Alfonso V installs his peripatetic court at Naples (1442). Lorenzo Valla, Beccadelli, Pontano and Manetti enter the royal household; the first Renaissance court north of Florence funded by an Iberian crown projects Aragonese soft power across Italy.

event.title: Alfonso the Magnanimous at Naples
event.text:
Naples has fallen, the Castel Nuovo flies the Senyera, and Alfonso V has installed his court in the city he fought five years to take. Lorenzo Valla (the philologist who proved the Donation of Constantine a forgery) sits in the king's pay. Antonio Beccadelli, called the Panormita, drafts the king's table-talk. Greek manuscripts arrive by the shipload from Constantinople in flight from the Ottomans. The court is suddenly the most brilliant on the Italian peninsula, more learned than Florence and more cosmopolitan than Rome.

But the same court hosts condottieri waiting for assignments, the king's military engineers studying gunpowder fortifications, and the bravos of the Italian Wars. Alfonso must decide where the patronage flows: into the humanist project that will outlast his name, or into the army of Mediterranean professionals that will keep his crown standing while he is alive.

options.text: The library of Naples: humanism above arms

modifiers.name: Lorenzo Valla's Naples
modifiers.text: The Magnanimous court chooses humanism. Valla works on his Elegantiae, Beccadelli compiles the king's witty sayings, and royal scriptoria copy Greek manuscripts. Aragonese soft power radiates north into Tuscany and beyond.

options.text: The arsenal of Naples: soldiers above scribes

modifiers.name: Patronage of Arms
modifiers.text: The Magnanimous court patronizes condottieri, military engineers and the Italian Wars officer class. Aragonese gold flows to the era's best soldiers, and Naples becomes the proving ground of the Mediterranean profession of arms.

advances.name: Drassanes Reials
advances.text: The Royal Shipyards of Barcelona (Gothic naval architecture able to lay down thirty galleys simultaneously under a single roof) become the industrial spine of Catalan-Aragonese sea power.

advances.name: Catalan Galley
advances.text: The signature warship of the Crown's Mediterranean dominance is standardized as a class. Faster than the Genoese galley, with reinforced hull for amphibious work, the Catalan galley protects the consulate convoys and lands the Almogavars on a hundred coasts.

advances.name: Catalan Galley Levy
advances.text: The Crown's Mediterranean port cities raise their own galley levies. Burghers of Barcelona, Valencia, Palma, Naples and Palermo finance the hulls; peasants and laborers along the Mediterranean shore row them. Mass-mobilization sea power without a standing fleet's cost.

advances.name: Senyera Consulates
advances.text: The Consols dels Catalans network covers every major Mediterranean port and stretches as far as Bruges and London. Each consulate flies the four-bar Senyera Reial and gives Catalan merchants extraterritorial protection under Aragonese commercial law.

advances.name: The Caricatori
advances.text: The grain of Sicily leaves the island through the royal loading ports: Sciacca, Girgenti, Licata, Termini. At each the master portolan weighs the cargo and sells the licence to export it, and the Crown's merchants carry the harvest to every shore of the inner sea.

advances.name: Mediterranean Viticulture
advances.text: The Penedès, Priorat, Sicilian, Campanian and Apulian wine regions all sit under the Aragonese crown. A continent-spanning wine economy unmatched by any single rival.

advances.name: Neapolitan Humanism
advances.text: After Alfonso V's death the cultural project he founded survives him: Pontano's Accademia, Sixtus Riessinger's Naples printing press (1471), and royal scriptoria sustain Aragonese humanism through the late 15th century.

advances.name: The Overseas Parliaments
advances.text: Sicily and Sardinia are given parliaments on the Catalan pattern, sitting in three arms: the barons, the prelates and the royal towns. A deputation of each realm watches over what was granted between sessions. A crown that is held to its pacts is voted its donatives.

advances.name: Tercio de Nápoles
advances.text: Gonzalo de Córdoba's reforms during the Italian Wars (1495-1504) produce the tercio: a combined-arms heavy infantry square fielding pike, sword and arquebus together. In our timeline the innovation flowers under Catalan-Aragonese rather than Castilian sponsorship.

advances.name: Royal Galiot
advances.text: The Drassanes Reials adapt the rowed warship to early modern conditions: a faster, lighter galiot for coast defense, convoy escort and the running anti-Ottoman skirmishes of the 16th-century Mediterranean.

advances.name: Consolat Supremacy
advances.text: The Catalan maritime code has become embedded as the Mediterranean lex maritima even where Aragonese flags no longer fly. The crown leverages the legal infrastructure for trade primacy.

advances.name: Pactist Resistance
advances.text: Aragonese jurists like Lluís de Peguera articulate the doctrine that constitutional pacts cannot be unilaterally abrogated by an absolutist crown. Tested in the Catalan Revolt of 1640 and the War of Spanish Succession, the doctrine grants the kingdom an unusual capacity for legal (and armed) resistance to royal overreach.

advances.name: Late Neapolitan Court
advances.text: Naples becomes one of the largest cities in Europe under the late Aragonese persistence. The patronage of Vico, Pergolesi and Galiani sustains Aragonese cultural primacy in southern Italy throughout the Enlightenment.

advances.name: Almadraba Fishery
advances.text: The almadraba bluefin tuna trap (Phoenician in origin, perfected by Catalan-Sicilian fishermen) becomes the largest organized pre-modern fishery in the Mediterranean. Salted tuna export grows into a state-monopoly industry.

advances.name: Almoixerifat Reform
advances.text: The medieval Aragonese customs and treasury offices (almoixerifats, originally Andalusi institutions adopted by the reconquista crown) are rationalized along late-absolutist Italianate lines, modernizing tax collection and construction administration.

advances.name: Jocs Florals
advances.text: The Floral Games of Barcelona are restored in 1859, and every spring the poets of the Crown compete for the natural flower, the golden eglantine and the golden violet. Aribau's Oda a la Patria and Verdaguer's Atlàntida are read aloud to crowds, and a public sphere returns to the language of the Consolat de Mar.

event.title: La Renaixenca
event.text: Bonaventura Aribau publishes the Oda a la Patria. Jacint Verdaguer prepares the Atlantida. The Jocs Florals are restored at Barcelona, and Catalan begins its return from kitchen and tavern to printing press, university and parliament floor. What was for two centuries the regional dialect of a peripheral province becomes once more the language of a literature, a politics, a public sphere. The vernacular of the Consolat de Mar finds its modern voice, and behind it, a national project.

advances.name: Indianas Industry
advances.text: Catalonia's printed-cotton industry (the indianas) scales into the first mechanized textile manufactories in Iberia. Barcelona becomes 'la fàbrica de Espanya,' the industrial workshop of the Aragonese crown.

advances.name: Companyies de Catalans
advances.text: The late-19th-century joint-stock companies (Banc de Barcelona, Companyia Trasatlàntica, La Maquinista Terrestre i Marítima) that finance Catalan industrial expansion and turn the crown's capital markets into the financial spine of southern European industrialization.

advances.name: Modernisme
advances.text: Gaudí, Domènech i Montaner, Puig i Cadafalch. The Renaixença's literary revival blossoms into a built civilization that defines Barcelona as one of the major centers of European modern art.

destiny.name: Imperial Project
destiny.text: The crown that has been formed must now choose what kind of empire it intends to become. The road forks: an eastern Mediterranean thalassocracy, or an Atlantic colonial power. Stability above 75 keeps the kingdom united for the choice.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Imperial Project
event.text: The royal council in Barcelona has settled the question. The kingdom is one, the throne is one, the project is one, and the path forward will now be measured in concrete objectives, not in the abstractions of court rhetoric. The chronicle of what the Crown of Aragon shall become opens a new chapter, and the king's secretaries set their pens to it.

destiny.name: Recover Catalan Greece
destiny.text: Reclaim the Duchy of Athens, the Duchy of Neopatras, and the Aragonese county of Patras, the Catalan Company's eastern conquests of 1303-1311. Own Athens, Neopatras and Patras, and hold a thousand gold to fund the expedition.

conditions.text: Mediterraneum Aragonense path chosen
Own Athína, or a subject owns it
Own Neái Pátra, or a subject owns it
Own Pátra, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: The Duchies Restored
event.text: Athens has fallen. Neopatras has bowed. The Aragonese banner flies once more over the Acropolis where the Catalan Company under Roger de Flor first raised it in 1311, a claim two centuries old, dormant since the Florentine Acciaiuoli evicted the last Catalan duke in 1388, now made good with steel. The chronicle of Ramon Muntaner is reread aloud at court. The eastern frontier of the Crown has reopened.

destiny.name: Aegean Empire
destiny.text: Take the strategic island arc that severs the eastern Mediterranean: Crete (Candia), Rhodes, and Chios. Field an army of fifty thousand men and build up Naples, the capital of the eastern venture, to make the conquest stick.

conditions.text: Own Candia, or a subject owns it
Own Ródos, or a subject owns it
Own Chíos, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50
We own Naples and its development is at least 57

event.title: The Aegean Garrisoned
event.text:
Candia, Rhodes, Chios (the strategic island chain of the eastern Mediterranean) all bow to the four bars. Venetian galleys must now ask permission to pass; Genoese factors petition the Crown for trade licenses; Mamluk envoys arrive in Naples to sound out terms. The kingdom has the islands. The question is what kind of empire to administer them as.

The military council wants strong garrisons in every island citadel: Aragonese soldiers, Catalan officers, the Acropolis at Athens turned back into a fortress as in the Catalan Company days. The chancellery prefers the Venetian model: bailiffs and consuls, hands-off rule, integration of the Greek and Latin populations through privilege rather than presence.

modifiers.name: Acropolis Garrison
modifiers.text: Aragonese soldiers in every island citadel from Athens to Rhodes. Catalan officers, Aragonese sergeants, fortress garrisons drilled in the old Almogavar tradition. Hard to dislodge, but reinforcing them across the eastern Mediterranean costs a great deal more than reinforcing the home fronts.

modifiers.name: Catalan Bailiwicks
modifiers.text: The Venetian model: light-touch rule through bailiffs, consuls, and locally co-opted Greek and Latin elites. The Senyera flies but does not garrison. Diplomacy substitutes for occupation.

destiny.name: Mare Nostrum Aragonense
destiny.text: The Mediterranean is the Crown's lake. Hold Famagusta on Cyprus, Alexandria in Egypt, and Tunis at the choke point of the inner sea. Three thousand gold, seventy-five prestige and a Barcelona grown into the home port of the inner sea mark the apex. Unlocks the Drassanes Maxima.

conditions.text: Own Famagusta, or a subject owns it
Own Alexandria, or a subject owns it
Own Tunis, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75
We own Barcelona and its development is at least 60

event.title: Mare Nostrum
event.text:
Famagusta, Alexandria, Tunis. The three terminals of the eastern Mediterranean trade triangle all fly the Senyera. The pilots of Genoa and Venice file their cargoes through Catalan consulates; the Mamluk sultanate has either fallen or come to terms; the Maghreb pays the Crown's tribute. There has not been a Mediterranean power of this scale since Rome.

The court must now decide what to do with such a position. The Pope offers a crusade title and the right to call any expedition against the Ottomans a holy war. The merchant houses of Barcelona prefer that the king consolidate the peace and turn the inner sea into a free Aragonese trading lake under a single administered customs system.

options.text: Take the crusader cross: finish the work.

modifiers.name: Crusader Aragon
modifiers.text: The Pope grants the crusade title. Aragonese arms turn Mediterranean dominance into a holy war against the Ottomans, the Mamluks, and the Maghreb. Tactical edge against unbelievers, paid for in war exhaustion among the Crown's Christian subjects.

effects.name: War Score vs other Religion Efficiency

modifiers.name: Sea King's Peace
modifiers.text: The Mediterranean becomes a single administered customs zone under Aragonese arbitration. The merchant houses of Barcelona prosper, the army costs less to keep, and peace settlements are negotiated from a position of unquestioned regional supremacy.

destiny.name: Atlantic Bridgehead
destiny.text: Seize the Atlantic staging archipelagos: the Canaries (Teguise), Madeira (Funchal) and the Azores (Ponta Delgada). With a thousand gold in reserve, the Crown turns its sailing tradition outward through the Pillars of Hercules.

conditions.text: Hispano-Aragonese path chosen
Own Teguise, or a subject owns it
Own Funchal, or a subject owns it
Own Ponta Delgada, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: The Pillars Crossed
event.text: The Canaries are Aragonese. Madeira is Aragonese. The Azores are Aragonese. Three archipelagos in a stepping-stone chain across the Atlantic (the same chain that in another timeline Castile used to reach the Indies) are now the Crown's bridgehead. Catalan sailors who have spent two centuries learning the Mediterranean carry that science out through the Strait of Gibraltar. The Western Ocean has become navigable space.

destiny.name: Catalan Caribbean
destiny.text: Plant the four bars over Hispaniola (Bohio) and Cuba (La Habana), raise La Habana into a town where the Indies fleets gather for the crossing home, and build up Palma, whose chartmakers and captains first sailed for the ocean islands. The first Catalan-Aragonese plantation Atlantic.

conditions.text: Own Habana, or a subject owns it
Own Bohio, or a subject owns it
La Habana is ours and has grown into a town or larger
We own Palma and its development is at least 35

event.title: The Catalan Indies
event.text:
Hispaniola is the Crown's. Cuba is the Crown's. La Habana flies the four bars rather than the lions and castles. The first Aragonese-Catalan plantations are set out, Catalan emigrants disembark at the new docks, and the question of how to administer the Indies becomes urgent.

The military adventurers (the conquistadors) petition the king for charters to conquer mainland kingdoms in his name. The clergy and the chancellery want a more orderly system: encomiendas administered through licensed grants, missionary orders training a converted indigenous labor force, and the Crown holding a tighter rein on its colonial captains.

modifiers.name: Conquistadors Catalans
modifiers.text: The Crown grants conquest charters to military adventurers from Catalonia, Valencia and Naples. The mainland indigenous kingdoms fall to small bands of cannon-bearing Catalan-Aragonese captains, at the price of the inflation that bullion shocks always bring.

modifiers.name: Catalan Encomienda
modifiers.text: Licensed encomienda grants administered through missionary orders. Conversion of the indigenous population proceeds through schools and parishes; colonial subjects integrate into the Crown's realm under the same constitutional pacts that govern Catalonia, Valencia and Naples.

destiny.name: Catalan Atlantic Empire
destiny.text: Reach the mainland: Tenochtitlan (the Mexica capital), Calamari (Cartagena de Indias) and Mayapan (Yucatan) all under Catalan-Aragonese sponsorship. Three thousand gold, seventy-five prestige and a Valencia grown rich on financing the voyages. Unlocks the Casa de Contratacio Catalana.

conditions.text: Own Tenōchtitlan, or a subject owns it
Own Calamari, or a subject owns it
Own Màayapáan, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75
We own Valencia and its development is at least 73

event.title: The Casa de Contratacio
event.text:
Tenochtitlan has fallen. The Yucatan is administered. Calamari sends its emerald and gold convoys up to Barcelona under Catalan flags. The Atlantic empire is now a fact, and the Crown founds in Barcelona the Casa de Contratacio Catalana, the trade administration that will license every voyage to the Indies, levy the royal fifth on every cargo, and adjudicate every colonial dispute under the Consolat de Mar.

The court debates how to run the system. The merchants of Barcelona, Valencia and Palma want a tightly licensed monopoly trade: Indies bullion flowing through a few designated ports under fixed customs schedules. The Trastamara administrators see otherwise: open the colonial system to Catalan migration, integrate the colonies into the realm as overseas kingdoms, raise their development the way Naples and Sicily were raised.

options.text: Monopoly trade: the Indies for the Crown.

modifiers.name: Indies Trade Monopoly
modifiers.text: The Casa de Contratacio licenses every voyage. Indies bullion flows through Barcelona, Valencia and Palma under tight customs control. Diplomatic capacity expands and wars become cheaper to declare, but the Crown's prestige decays slightly as the imperial project becomes a commercial enterprise rather than a chivalric one.

modifiers.name: Atlantic Dominion
modifiers.text: The colonies are integrated as overseas kingdoms, like Naples or Sicily, only across the Ocean. Catalan emigrants raise plantations and cities; the Crown's standing among the great powers is recognized; population growth and colonial recovery are accelerated by the open settlement system.

units.name: Catalan Galley
units.text: The standardized warship of the Crown's Mediterranean fleet. Reinforced for amphibious work, faster than its Genoese rivals, designed to convoy Catalan commerce and disembark Almogavars on hostile beaches.

units.name: Catalan Levy Galley
units.text: Coastal-burgher levy variant of the Catalan galley, raised from the port cities of Barcelona, Valencia, Palma, Naples and Palermo. Crewed by laborers and peasants from the Mediterranean shore.

units.name: Royal Galiot
units.text: The Drassanes Reials' early-modern evolution of the galley, a lighter, faster rowed vessel for coast defense and anti-Ottoman skirmishing in the late Mediterranean wars.

units.name: Tercio de Nápoles
units.text: The combined-arms infantry square forged in Aragonese Naples during the Italian Wars: pike, sword and arquebus integrated into a single tactical unit. The most disciplined heavy infantry in 16th-century Europe.

buildings.name: Caricatore
buildings.text: A royal loading port on the Sicilian model. Grain is stored in pits cut above the quay, weighed by the master portolan and shipped under a licence bought from the Crown. Buyers' factors from every port of the inner sea keep a table here.

buildings.name: Hall of the Three Arms
buildings.text: The house where the three arms of a realm's parliament meet: the barons, the prelates and the syndics of the royal towns. The donative is voted here, and the Crown is held to its sworn pacts.

buildings.name: Magnanimous Court
buildings.text: The peripatetic Renaissance court founded by Alfonso V at Naples in 1442. Lorenzo Valla, Beccadelli, Pontano and Manetti served here; royal scriptoria copied Greek manuscripts arriving in flight from the falling Eastern Empire.

buildings.name: Almudín
buildings.text: Valencia's great Gothic covered granary, expanded across the Crown's cities. Centralized food storage, fair-price grain markets, and supply infrastructure for Mediterranean campaigning.

buildings.name: Drassanes Reials
buildings.text: The Royal Shipyards of Barcelona: preserved Gothic naval architecture, capable of laying down up to thirty galleys simultaneously under a single covered roof. The industrial spine of Catalan-Aragonese sea power.

buildings.name: Senyera Consulate
buildings.text: A Catalan consulate of the Consols dels Catalans network, flying the four-bar Senyera Reial. Grants extraterritorial protection to the Crown's merchants and applies Aragonese commercial law in the host port.

buildings.name: Mediterranean Vineyard
buildings.text: A vineyard of the Penedès, Priorat, Sicilian, Campanian or Apulian growing regions, planted and kept by its tenants so that the land bears more wine. The Crown's wines move along the Catalan trade network from Bruges to Constantinople.

where.text: The location's raw material is Wine

buildings.name: Almadraba
buildings.text: The Catalan-Sicilian almadraba bluefin tuna trap. Industrial-scale fishery feeding the Mediterranean salted-tuna export market, one of the largest pre-modern protein industries in Europe.

where.text: The location's raw material is Fish

buildings.name: Catalan Cotton Mill
buildings.text: Barcelona's printed-cotton manufactory. The indianas industry mechanized: la fàbrica de Espanya, the industrial workshop of the late Aragonese crown.

buildings.name: Drassanes Maxima
buildings.text: The imperial-scale evolution of the Drassanes Reials. A grand Mediterranean naval headquarters constructed under the Mare Nostrum project, capable of laying down four warships at once and sustaining the Crown's eastern fleet from a single dockyard.

buildings.name: Casa de Contratacio Catalana
buildings.text: Barcelona's parallel to the Castilian Casa de Contratacion. Licenses every voyage to the Indies, levies the royal fifth on bullion cargoes, registers Catalan emigrants, and adjudicates colonial commercial disputes under the Consolat de Mar, the Crown's imperial trade administration.

list.name: Reial Cancelleria d'Aragó
list.text: The Aragonese royal chancery, professionalized under Jaume II from c.1290 and codified by Pere III's 1344 Ordinacions de la Casa Reial. Staffed by university-trained letrats, it issues decrees in Catalan, Aragonese, Latin, and (from Alfonso V) Italian, maintaining one of medieval Europe's most disciplined diplomatic registries, the foundation of Catalan literary prose and the Crown's administrative coherence across four kingdoms separated by sea.

list.name: Corts Generals de Montsó
list.text: The general parliament of the whole Crown, first gathered at Monzón in 1289. The town lies on the border of Aragon and Catalonia, so Aragonese, Catalans and Valencians can be summoned to one place without any of them leaving the Crown's own ground for a foreign realm. Each sits apart and votes by its own laws, and the king hears their grievances before a donative is granted. One summons serves every realm, and none of them is bound by what another conceded.

conditions.text: Owns Monzón

list.name: Consolat de Mar
list.text: The Mediterranean's first maritime jurisdiction, chartered at Valencia in 1283 by Pere III the Great and codified in the Llibre del Consolat de Mar, whose articles govern shipowner liability, crew wages, and prize cases from Barcelona to Messina to Trapani. By the fifteenth century its Catalan-language jurisprudence is the lingua franca of Mediterranean commerce, cited in Genoese and Venetian courts and translated into every major Mediterranean language.

list.name: Regia Camera della Sommaria
list.text: The supreme accounting court of the Kingdom of Naples, expanded by Alfonso V the Magnanimous after his 1442 conquest from a thirteenth-century Angevin nucleus. Its luogotenenti and razionali audit every demesne revenue, customs duty, and feudal due from Abruzzo to Calabria, providing the fiscal backbone that funds Alfonso's humanist court at Castel Nuovo and his Italian wars. Naples becomes the workshop of late-medieval Aragonese statecraft.

conditions.text: Owns Naples
